summary:
Greenland is a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark. Its parliament and courts handle domestic affairs, while the criminal law that applies here is Denmark's Criminal Code, extended to Greenland. Same-sex relations are lawful.

Greenland's record on partnership and marriage has been permissive for three decades. A registered partnership law modeled on the Danish statute took effect on 1 July 1996 and passed with virtually no debate in the local parliament. It was repealed when the same-sex marriage law took effect on 1 April 2016.

Same-sex marriage arrived through adoption of Danish legislation that had passed the Danish parliament unanimously twice; the first bill lapsed after Danish elections. Greenland's parliament enacted the measure without recorded opposition, and the bishop of the established church supported it.

Hate speech has been criminalised since 2010. Article 100 of the Criminal Code prohibits speech that may deprive, threaten or demean people on the basis of sexual orientation among other categories, and the code carries penalty enhancements for hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation.

Greenland's parliament passed a Law on Equal Treatment and Anti-Discrimination in May 2024, in force from 1 July 2024. It prohibits discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and gender characteristics, establishes an Equal Treatment Board to handle discrimination complaints, and creates an Equality Council to promote non-discrimination. The state-funded Human Rights Council of Greenland works closely with the Danish Institute for Human Rights.

Transgender residents can change the sex designation on official identity documents under a 2016 decree-based law resting on self-determination. No sex reassignment surgery, hormone therapy, sterilisation or medical diagnosis is required. Applicants must be over 18 and state that they want their documentation changed, then observe a six-month reflection period to confirm the request. Greenlandic passports carry an "X" sex descriptor alongside male and female.

The social climate is low-key. Gay life is described as almost a non-event: integrated, and non-violent. There is virtually no gay scene, a consequence of the small and scattered population, though some nightclubs and bars in Nuuk draw a mixed gay and straight crowd. The first pride parade in Nuuk was held on 15 May 2010 and drew about 1,000 people; a modest Pride march has run annually since.

Organised advocacy exists. In August 2014 the national association LGBT Qaamaneq was founded for lesbians, gays, bisexuals and transgender people, working for political, cultural and social equality and open to family, friends and colleagues as supporters.
tangentialFactors:
Greenland's legal protections track Denmark's rather than diverging from it: the marriage statute was Danish legislation adopted locally, and the hate-speech provision is an article of the Danish Criminal Code. A visitor who knows the Danish position on any of these questions is starting from roughly the right baseline.

The trajectory is consistent across three decades. The 1996 partnership law passed without controversy, the 2016 marriage bill recorded no opposition, and the 2024 equality law added gender identity, gender expression and gender characteristics to a statutory list of protected grounds. No source in the inventory documents a legislative rollback or a contested vote on any of these measures.

Public visibility is limited by demography rather than by prohibition. Bars and nightclubs in Nuuk mix gay and straight patrons, and the annual Pride march draws a crowd of around a thousand, but the scattered population means there is no organised scene outside the capital.

Physical safety appears better than in many jurisdictions. Reports describe gay life as non-violent and non-controversial, and the inventory contains no account of a bias-motivated assault, killing or organised hostility against transgender people in Greenland.
localsOnly:
Residents discriminated against on a ground covered by the Law on Equal Treatment and Anti-Discrimination can bring a complaint to the Equal Treatment Board, the body the same law creates to manage such cases. The Equality Council operates alongside it on the promotion side of non-discrimination policy.

Legal gender recognition is a resident-facing process with fixed conditions: the applicant must be 18 or older, make a stated request to have documentation changed, and wait six months before the request is confirmed. The absence of any medical prerequisite removes the surgical, hormonal and diagnostic gatekeeping common elsewhere.

Advocacy and community infrastructure includes LGBT Qaamaneq, founded in August 2014 and explicitly open to family, friends and colleagues as supporters, alongside the annual Pride march in Nuuk that has run since 2010. The Human Rights Council of Greenland is state-funded and works with the Danish Institute for Human Rights.
outOfScopeNotes:
Entry and visa requirements for Greenland are not covered by any source in this inventory, including whether a separate authorisation is needed beyond permission to enter Denmark and the Schengen area. Unresolved.

How Article 100 of the Criminal Code is applied in practice in Greenlandic courts is not sourced here. The inventory gives the text of the provision and its protected categories but no case, prosecution or penalty actually imposed. Unresolved.

The hate-crime penalty enhancements are described only in relation to sexual orientation. Whether they also reach offences motivated by gender identity or gender expression is not stated in the sources. Not sourced.

Enforcement of the Law on Equal Treatment and Anti-Discrimination since it took effect on 1 July 2024 is not documented here: no complaint figures, board decisions or reported refusals of service. Unresolved.

Denmark's own gender-recognition statute, and how its terms interact with Greenland's 2016 decree-based process for someone holding Danish rather than Greenlandic documents, is not addressed in the inventory. Unresolved.

No source covers detention or prison placement by gender identity, access to transition-related healthcare, school anti-bullying policy, or rules on access to sex-segregated facilities. Not sourced.
